title: Trump Rolls Back Biden-Era Fuel Economy Rules, Calling Them an 'EV Mandate'
summary: President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he is rolling back fuel economy standards adopted under former President Joe Biden, arguing the change will lower car prices and boost American manufacturing. In a social media post, Trump said the new standards would "TERMINATE" what he called Biden's "EV mandate" — though there is no federal law requiring Americans to buy electric vehicles. At the center of the debate are Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, established by Congress in 1975. These rules require automakers to meet average fuel economy targets across all cars and light trucks they sell. Under Biden-era rules finalized in 2024, the required fleetwide average was set to rise from 39.1 miles per gallon (mpg) to about 50.4 mpg by 2031. The Biden administration said the rules would cut fuel consumption and emissions to fight climate change while saving drivers money at the pump. Trump did not provide exact numbers for his new standards, but in December 2025 he proposed a fleetwide average of roughly 34.5 mpg by 2031 — more than 30 percent lower than Biden's rule. "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car," Trump wrote. The Republican-controlled Congress already gutted consumer tax incentives for electric vehicles last year as part of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an announcement would be "COMING MONDAY." Supporters say the rollback helps carmakers and buyers. Critics argue it will increase pollution and widen the gap between U.S. policy and global trends favoring electric vehicles.
why_it_matters: Fuel economy rules decide what kinds of cars get built and sold for the next decade, which shapes the price you might pay for a first car, how much money goes to oil producers, and how much carbon the country adds to the atmosphere. The gap between U.S. rules and stricter European and Chinese targets also affects which automakers stay competitive globally.

background_read: CAFE (Corporate Average Fuel Economy) standards were created by Congress in 1975, shortly after the 1973 oil embargo, when oil-producing countries cut off supplies to the United States and drivers faced long lines at gas stations. The rules were designed to make the U.S. less dependent on foreign oil, and they have been tightened and loosened by different administrations ever since.

It's worth knowing that CAFE is not a ban on any type of vehicle: it sets an average that each automaker's whole fleet must hit, so a company can still sell large trucks and SUVs if it also sells efficient cars. That's why the standards are a favorite target of political fights — they quietly shape what gets built, what gets sold and what consumers pay.

Joe Biden (U.S. president from 2021 to 2025) made electric vehicles a centerpiece of his climate agenda, while Donald Trump (president again since 2025) has pushed to expand oil and gas production and to undo many Biden-era climate rules. The U.S. is not alone in regulating fuel: the European Union and China both have stricter emissions targets, and several countries have announced plans to stop selling new gasoline cars in the 2030s.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — cheaper cars, stronger domestic manufacturing
perspectives.description: Supporters argue that requiring less-efficient cars to meet tough averages forces automakers to spend billions on technology, and that cost shows up in sticker prices. They say looser standards let companies build the vehicles Americans actually buy, keep factories busy and save families thousands of dollars.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — more pollution and a drift from global trends
perspectives.description: Critics point out that weaker standards mean more gasoline burned and more emissions, undermining climate goals. They also warn that if U.S. automakers plan for lower efficiency while Europe and China push electric vehicles harder, American companies could fall behind in the global market they will need in the 2030s.

CAFE standards have swung back and forth between administrations since the 1970s, so this rollback fits a long pattern rather than a one-off event. The key structural question is that Congress wrote the rules in the first place, meaning lasting change usually requires legislation, not just a new announcement.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — the numbers still to come
perspectives.description: Trump gave no final figures, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said details were coming soon, so the practical effect is still unknown. Watch whether the final rule survives legal challenges, and whether automakers respond by redesigning their lineups or by waiting for the next administration to reverse course again.
